# Batch dosing -- TIA Portal starter

*Generated by `tools/gen_starters.py` from the scene's tag set. Do not edit by
hand; regenerate. The function block's body is yours.*

**The task.** Dose the number of litres on the panel's pot into the tank, then transfer the batch out. Do it with two loops: an inner one that trims pump.speed until meter.rate is the dosing rate you want, and an outer one that watches meter.total and decides what that rate should be — full rate at first, tapering over the last few litres so the cut-off does not carry you past the number. Zero the totaliser before each batch, and remember its reset is a level, not an edge.

**Done when.** The batch lands within a litre or two of the pot, and the tank agrees: 20 L into a 200 L tank is 10 % of level, measured by an instrument that is not the meter. Then halve your dosing rate and run the same recipe — the same litres, in about twice the time. A batch timed in seconds would have delivered half. Finally fail the pump mid-dose (pump.fault) and watch pump.speed hold at whatever you commanded while meter.rate collapses: the flow loop knows within two seconds, and the level will not have moved a whole percent.

## Set it up

1. In a project with an S7-1500 CPU: *External source files -> Add new
   external file*, pick `batch_dosing.scl`, then right-click it -> *Generate
   blocks from source*. That creates `FF_IO` and `"BatchDosing"`. One
   exercise per CPU: this `FF_IO` replaces any other one.
2. Call `"BatchDosing"` from OB1 (drag it into `Main`; TIA creates the
   instance DB).
3. Check `FF_IO`'s properties: *Optimized block access* off (the source sets
   it), *Accessible from HMI/OPC UA* and *Writable from HMI/OPC UA* on for
   every member (TIA's default). Without *Writable* every sensor reads FALSE
   forever.
4. Compile, download, RUN.

## Run it

Open the scene in FactoryForge first (pick "Batch dosing" on the start screen (or launch with --scene=res://templates/batch_dosing.json)), then attach
the sidecar with whichever driver reaches your CPU:

```bash
factoryforge-sidecar connect --driver opcua-client --mapping examples/tia/batch-dosing/opcua_mapping.json -o url opc.tcp://<cpu-ip>:4840
factoryforge-sidecar connect --driver s7-snap7 -o host <cpu-ip> -o db <FF_IO's number> --mapping examples/tia/batch-dosing/snap7_mapping.json
factoryforge-sidecar connect --driver plcsim-advanced -o instance <name> --mapping examples/tia/batch-dosing/plcsim_mapping.json
```

(From a source checkout: `python -m factoryforge_sidecar` in place of
`factoryforge-sidecar`, run from the repository root so the paths resolve.)
To have it marked, run `python tools/grade.py --scene batch-dosing` in place
of the 3D scene and add the `--port` it prints to the same command.

The OPC UA namespace index is usually 3, not always: run
`factoryforge-sidecar browse opc.tcp://<cpu-ip>:4840` once and fix `ns=` in
the mapping if yours differs.

## FF_IO

In declaration order. `PLC writes` is an output (a motor, a valve, a lamp);
`PLC reads` is an input (a sensor, a button, a measurement). The two
directions never share a byte, so the snap7 driver never rewrites a bit your
program owns. `FF_IO` is 48 bytes. *Brief* marks the signals the task
names.

| Tag | Direction | Member | Type | Offset | Meaning | Brief |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `flow_gauge.value` | PLC writes | `FlowGaugeValue` | Real | DBD0 | needle position, scale 0..150 L/min | yes |
| `level_readout.value` | PLC writes | `LevelReadoutValue` | DInt | DBD4 | number shown on the display (%) | yes |
| `pump.speed` | PLC writes | `PumpSpeed` | Real | DBD8 | speed reference, 0..100 % | yes |
| `tank.drain` | PLC writes | `TankDrain` | Real | DBD12 | drain valve opening, 0..100 % | yes |
| `tank.fill` | PLC writes | `TankFill` | Real | DBD16 | fill valve opening, 0..100 % |  |
| `total_display.value` | PLC writes | `TotalDisplayValue` | DInt | DBD20 | number shown on the display (L) | yes |
| `meter.reset` | PLC writes | `MeterReset` | Bool | DBX24.0 | a LEVEL: held TRUE keeps the total at zero | yes |
| `panel.green` | PLC writes | `PanelGreen` | Bool | DBX24.1 | green lamp on the panel | yes |
| `panel.red` | PLC writes | `PanelRed` | Bool | DBX24.2 | red lamp on the panel | yes |
| `pump.run` | PLC writes | `PumpRun` | Bool | DBX24.3 | run the pump | yes |
| `tower.green` | PLC writes | `TowerGreen` | Bool | DBX24.4 | tower lamp, green |  |
| `tower.red` | PLC writes | `TowerRed` | Bool | DBX24.5 | tower lamp, red |  |
| `tower.yellow` | PLC writes | `TowerYellow` | Bool | DBX24.6 | tower lamp, yellow |  |
| `meter.rate` | PLC reads | `MeterRate` | Real | DBD26 | measured flow rate, L/min | yes |
| `meter.total` | PLC reads | `MeterTotal` | DInt | DBD30 | litres since the last reset, whole litres | yes |
| `panel.setpoint` | PLC reads | `PanelSetpoint` | Real | DBD34 | the operator's pot, 5..60 L (starts at 20) | yes |
| `pump.flow` | PLC reads | `PumpFlow` | Real | DBD38 | measured flow, L/min -- the measurement, not the command | yes |
| `tank.level` | PLC reads | `TankLevel` | Real | DBD42 | tank level, % of capacity | yes |
| `panel.estop` | PLC reads | `PanelEstop` | Bool | DBX46.0 | E-stop, normally closed: TRUE = healthy, FALSE = pressed; stays pressed until pulled out | yes |
| `panel.reset` | PLC reads | `PanelReset` | Bool | DBX46.1 | Reset button, momentary: a short pulse per press | yes |
| `panel.start` | PLC reads | `PanelStart` | Bool | DBX46.2 | Start button, momentary: a short pulse per press -- latch it | yes |
| `panel.stop` | PLC reads | `PanelStop` | Bool | DBX46.3 | Stop button, momentary: a short pulse per press | yes |
| `pump.fault` | PLC reads | `PumpFault` | Bool | DBX46.4 | motor fault: TRUE = failed; it reports your command and delivers nothing | yes |
| `tank.fault` | PLC reads | `TankFault` | Bool | DBX46.5 | valve fault: TRUE = a valve has seized and holds its opening, whatever you command |  |

`int` travels as a `DInt` and `float` as a `Real`: the OPC UA driver writes
Int32 and Float, and a member of any other type is refused as a type mismatch.
Hold anything the scene must see for well over a second on OPC UA: an
S7-1500 forces a 1000 ms publishing interval on subscriptions, which is why the
driver polls by default.
